Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The current imaging shows a partial response with three lesions disappearing and the remaining lesions reduced by about 40 %. However, decisive information required to confirm technical resectability is missing: precise anatomic distribution of the residual lesions (bilobar vs. unilobar, proximity to major vessels or biliary structures), quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume, baseline liver function and any chemotherapy‑associated liver injury, and the presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease. Until these data are obtained, a definitive “Resectable upfront” or “Not resectable” classification cannot be made, making the case “Potentially resectable” pending further assessment.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Continue the current FOLFOXIRI regimen (or complete the planned number of cycles) to maximize tumor shrinkage and to use response as a biological test of disease aggressiveness.  
- At the end of the neoadjuvant phase (typically after 6–8 cycles, ≈2–3 months), repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and obtain a contrast‑enhanced CT for volumetric analysis.  
- Perform a dedicated liver volumetry study to calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % in the setting of chemotherapy‑injured liver (or < 20 % in a normal liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy.  
- Simultaneously reassess the rectal primary: if symptomatic (bleeding, obstruction) or high‑risk T4 disease, schedule neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by primary resection; if asymptomatic, a liver‑first approach is acceptable.  
- Multidisciplinary review of the updated imaging to map each residual metastasis; aim for an R0 resection while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
- If all lesions can be cleared with adequate FLR, proceed to curative‑intent hepatic resection (potentially extended right or left hepatectomy, or combined segmental resections) possibly combined with intra‑operative ablation for lesions in difficult locations.  
- Post‑operative plan: 3–6 months of adjuvant systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI or a doublet plus targeted agent based on molecular profile) and, if indicated, postoperative pelvic radiotherapy for the rectal primary.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and liver volumetry data.  
- Exact segmental location of each residual liver lesion and relationship to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
- Baseline liver function tests and assessment of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (e.g., steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Performance status and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI) to guide targeted therapy decisions.  
- Details of the rectal primary (T stage, nodal status, symptoms, prior radiotherapy).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Both recommendations address the same clinical domains and management components such as resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy and surveillance. They both classify the case as 'potentially resectable,' require further imaging and volumetric assessment, and recommend continued systemic therapy with potential surgical intervention based on resectability after re-evaluation.

In terms of step concordance, both recommendations follow a similar sequence: assessing resectability as 'potentially resectable,' recommending further imaging and evaluation, continuing systemic therapy, and planning surgery if resectability criteria are met.

For case-tailoring concordance, both recommendations specify detailed, patient-specific factors such as the exact mapping of liver lesions, assessment of FLR, potential need for portal vein embolization, and specific surgical strategies if resectability is confirmed. They also consider molecular profiling for systemic therapy adaptation.

Regarding missing data, both recommendations identify similar essential information gaps, including exact lesion mapping, FLR, presence of extrahepatic disease, and the tumor's molecular profile, among others. Although the lists are not identical, there is significant overlap, indicating concordance in recognizing critical missing information.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The post‑chemotherapy MRI shows three residual metastases each <2 cm, which from a purely oncologic view could be amenable to curative‑intent resection. However, technical feasibility cannot be confirmed without decisive information that is currently missing:  

- Precise segmental location of each lesion and their relationship to the hepatic veins, portal pedicles and biliary structures (needed to guarantee an R0 margin while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments).  
- Quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume or FLR/body‑weight ratio (>30 % or >0.5 % respectively) to ensure adequate postoperative liver function.  

Because these data are essential to determine whether a safe, margin‑negative hepatectomy can be performed, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending further evaluation (or a prerequisite intervention such as portal vein embolization if FLR proves insufficient).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

- Continue systemic therapy to complete a standard peri‑operative course (e.g., total 6 – 8 cycles of a doublet regimen such as FOLFOX or FOLFIRI combined with anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS‑wild‑type status). This consolidates tumor response and provides additional “proof of time” for disease biology.  
- At cycle 6 (or earlier if imaging suggests maximal response), repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and obtain a volumetric CT to:  
   • Re‑map lesion locations, confirm absence of new intra‑ or extra‑hepatic disease (including chest CT).  
   • Calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to induce hypertrophy.  
- If imaging confirms that all three lesions can be resected with negative margins while preserving adequate FLR, schedule curative‑intent liver surgery. Preferred approach: anatomic or non‑anatomic resections tailored to lesion distribution, using intra‑operative ultrasound to detect any occult disease.  
- Simultaneously address the primary rectal tumor: if the rectal lesion is still in situ and resectable, plan a combined or staged colorectal resection (e.g., low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision) after liver surgery, depending on patient fitness and operative risk.  
- Post‑operative management:  
   • Pathologic assessment of resection margins; if R0 achieved, proceed with adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 3–6 months of the same doublet ± biologic) to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
   • Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then semi‑annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  

- Exact segmental location of each hepatic lesion and proximity to major vessels/biliary structures.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (or FLR/body‑weight ratio).  
- Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine‑green clearance (if available) to assess hepatic reserve.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (e.g., cardiovascular, pulmonary).  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (already resected, in situ, symptomatic) and any local staging (MRI pelvis).  
- Comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT/PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary or peritoneal disease.  
- Molecular profile beyond RAS (BRAF, MSI/dMMR) which may influence adjuvant choices.  

These items are essential to finalize resectability and to tailor the definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
1. **Completeness**: Both recommendations address the resectability assessment, imaging, systemic therapy, and surgical management. However, they differ significantly in their approach and details, particularly in how each handles disappeared metastases and the integration of rectal primary management. Recommendation 1 focuses more on completing a chemotherapy regimen and re-evaluation prior to surgery, while Recommendation 2 emphasizes restaging and strategic planning for the original metastatic map. Additionally, Recommendation 2 includes prehabilitation and ERAS protocols which are not mentioned in Recommendation 1. Therefore, they do not cover the same domains comprehensively.

2. **Step-by-step Concordance**: Recommendation 1 considers the case as potentially resectable pending further evaluation, while Recommendation 2 considers it resectable but requires detailed mapping and restaging, indicating a difference in the initial assessment of resectability. The proposed management plans also differ; Recommendation 1 suggests a peri-operative chemotherapy course and then evaluates for surgery, while Recommendation 2 outlines a more immediate restaging and potential surgical intervention, considering all metastatic sites, not just the visible ones.

3. **Case-tailoring Concordance**: Case-specific factors such as the original distribution of metastases, approach to disappeared metastases, and integration of rectal management are handled differently. Recommendation 2 specifically considers the original metastatic sites and uses this information to plan treatment, while Recommendation 1 does not emphasize this. Additionally, Recommendation 2 includes prehabilitation and ERAS protocols tailored to the patient's condition.

4. **Missing Data Concordance**: Both recommendations identify the need for segmental and vascular localization of hepatic lesions and future liver remnant estimation. However, Recommendation 2 additionally identifies the need for localization of disappeared metastases, CRM status on pelvic MRI, and liquid biopsies, which are not mentioned in Recommendation 1, indicating a difference in identified missing data.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Classification: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning  
- Current imaging shows 7 viable liver metastases (6 stable, 1 progressing 5 cm in segment VII). Number alone does not preclude resection if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
- No information is provided on:  
   • Total tumor volume and distribution across hepatic segments (bilobar vs unilobar).  
   • Proximity of lesions to major vascular or biliary structures.  
   • Calculated FLR percentage (≥30 % in chemotherapy‑treated livers is generally required).  
   • Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets, Child‑Pugh).  
   • Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
   • Status of the primary colon tumor (resected, symptomatic, need for neoadjuvant radiotherapy).  
Because FLR adequacy and anatomic feasibility are decisive for a curative hepatectomy, and these data are missing, the case cannot be labeled “Resectable upfront.” The presence of a single progressing lesion also suggests the need for additional down‑staging or local control before definitive surgery, fulfilling the definition of “Potentially resectable.”  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
1. Confirm staging completeness  
   - Perform high‑quality triphasic CT or MRI with liver‑specific contrast (e.g., Gd‑EOB‑MRI) to map all lesions, assess vascular involvement, and calculate FLR.  
   - Obtain PET‑CT (or high‑sensitivity MRI) to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

2. Systemic therapy continuation / optimisation  
   - Continue a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin backbone (FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF), since KRAS mutation predicts lack of benefit from EGFR antibodies.  
   - Consider adding a short course of irinotecan‑based regimen (FOLFIRI) if progression persists after 2–3 months.  

3. Targeted local treatment of the progressing lesion  
   - Evaluate the 5 cm segment VII lesion for suitability for percutaneous ablation (RFA or microwave) or stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT).  
   - If the lesion is adjacent to major vessels, consider Y‑90 radio‑embolization (SIRT) to achieve down‑staging while preserving liver parenchyma.  

4. Re‑assessment of resectability (≈6–8 weeks after the last systemic cycle)  
   - Repeat imaging, recalculate FLR.  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy) and all lesions are amenable to R0 resection, proceed to surgery.  

5. Surgical plan  
   - Liver‑first approach (reverse sequence) if the primary colon tumor is asymptomatic and the liver disease is the dominant threat.  
   - Perform an anatomic or non‑anatomic hepatectomy aiming for negative margins (≥ 1 mm, ideally ≥ 10 mm).  
   - If FLR is borderline, consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to induce hypertrophy before definitive resection.  
   - Combine resection with intra‑operative ablation for lesions that are technically unresectable but reachable.  

6. Management of the primary tumor  
   - If the colon primary has not been resected and is not causing obstruction or bleeding, schedule a curative colectomy either simultaneously (if hepatic resection is limited) or after hepatic surgery, based on operative risk and patient fitness.  

7. Adjuvant / peri‑operative therapy  
   - After R0 resection, resume the same systemic regimen (FOLFOX + bevacizumab) for 3–6 months, unless contraindicated.  
   - Enroll the patient in a clinical trial if available (e.g., conversion‑therapy protocols, liver‑directed therapies).  

Step 3 – Missing data essential for a reliable recommendation  
- Quantitative FLR calculation (volumetry) and liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count, Child‑Pugh score).  
- Detailed anatomic distribution of all liver lesions (segmental map, size of each stable lesion, relationship to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Performance status (ECOG/WHO), comorbidities, cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Current status of the primary colon tumor (resected, symptomatic, need for radiotherapy).  
- Exact systemic regimen already delivered, number of cycles, and response assessment (RECIST criteria).  
- Baseline tumor markers (CEA, CA 19‑9) trend.  

These data are required to finalize the decision on whether an immediate hepatectomy is feasible or whether further down‑staging, portal vein embolization, or staged surgery is needed.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
- Completeness: Both recommendations cover the same clinical domains including imaging, systemic therapy adjustments, local treatments, and FLR estimation. They both acknowledge the importance of mapping lesions and understanding the tumor's anatomical and biological characteristics. They address the need for preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and potential postoperative therapy.

- Step Concordance: The first recommendation considers the case 'potentially resectable' with a structured plan towards achieving resectability, involving systemic therapy, local ablative techniques, and surgical strategies. The second recommendation labels the disease 'unresectable' at this stage and focuses more on systemic control and a less aggressive resection/ablation approach. This represents a fundamental difference in the management pathway and ultimate goal setting (curative vs. cytoreductive), resulting in a lack of step concordance.

- Case Tailoring: Recommendation 1 is more tailored to specific patient and disease characteristics, such as KRAS mutation and chemotherapy history, guiding the choice of systemic therapy. Recommendation 2 mentions molecular profiling in the context of adjuvant therapy but does not integrate this into the upfront decision-making process. This results in a lack of alignment in case-specific tailoring.

- Missing Data Concordance: Both recommendations identify the same types of essential information needed to proceed: lesion distribution, FLR estimation, and the status of the primary colon tumor. While Recommendation 2 adds molecular profiling and liquid biopsies, these do not drastically diverge the focus from the primary missing data addressed in Recommendation 1. Hence, there is agreement in identifying critical missing data.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the patient has a radiological complete response after 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, but definitive surgical planning requires (a) precise knowledge of the original bilobar lesion locations and volumes to guide intra‑operative resection of the sites of occult disease, and (b) confirmation that an adequate future liver remnant (≥30 % of total liver volume or >0.5 % body weight) can be preserved. Without these pieces of information the liver cannot be declared resectable upfront.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Review pre‑treatment imaging (CT/MRI) to map each metastasis (segment, size, number) and calculate future liver remnant (CT volumetry).  
• Perform liver function assessment (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance if available) and assess patient fitness (ECOG/ASA).  
• Schedule surgery after a short interval (4–6 weeks) from the last chemotherapy cycle to allow hepatic recovery; no bevacizumab wash‑out is needed because it was not used.  
• Operative plan:  
   – Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate the prior metastatic sites.  
   – Perform anatomic or non‑anatomic resections (segmental, subsegmental, or wedge) of all previously involved areas, aiming for R0 resection of any residual microscopic disease while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   – If the rectal primary remains unresected and is technically resectable, consider a liver‑first approach (resect liver first, then low‑anterior resection 6–8 weeks later) or a simultaneous resection if operative risk is acceptable and the primary is low‑lying without need for extensive pelvic dissection.  
• Post‑operative systemic therapy: complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., resume FOLFOX or capecitabine‑oxaliplatin for the remaining cycles not yet given) to eradicate micrometastatic disease, as supported by the EORTC 40983 peri‑operative regimen.  
• Adjuvant treatment of the rectal primary according to standard rectal cancer guidelines (e.g., postoperative chemoradiation if indicated by margin or nodal status).  
• Surveillance: CEA and contrast‑enhanced MRI of the liver (or CT if MRI unavailable) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Exact number, size, and segmental distribution of the original liver metastases (pre‑treatment imaging).  
• Calculated future liver remnant volume and liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance).  
• Performance status, comorbidities, and ASA classification.  
• Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR).  
• Current status of the rectal primary (clinical T stage, response to any neoadjuvant radiotherapy, symptom burden).  
• Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung nodules) on the most recent staging scans.

Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the initial metastases relative to vascular structures.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor : circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
E. Patient’s performance status for potential staged hepatectomy.
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.

- **Completeness**: Both recommendations address the critical aspects of resectability assessment, imaging requisites (preoperative staging), systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy and surveillance. Each covers the need for detailed analysis of initial metastatic sites and future liver remnant estimation. Additionally, both provide guidance on systemic therapy and integrate the management of the rectal primary, albeit with different specifics. Therefore, they are complete with respect to covering the major clinical management components.

- **Step Concordance**: Recommendation 1 and Recommendation 2 diverge in their step-by-step management sequence. Recommendation 1 suggests a definitive surgical plan post-imaging and assessment, focusing on intra-operative ultrasound and R0 resection, with a possible liver-first approach. Recommendation 2, however, introduces more conditional steps, such as continuing systemic therapy or using local ablative techniques if surgery is not feasible, and a detailed breakdown of options based on rectal tumor response. Because of these differences in the surgical approach and management of the rectal primary, they do not align on a step-by-step basis.

Recommendation 1 includes molecular profile and comorbidities, while Recommendation 2 mentions liquid biopsies and detailed vascular localization of metastases. Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
Reasoning: • Single 3.9 cm metastasis confined to segment VII, no extra‑hepatic disease on CT. • Prior bisegmentectomy IV‑V leaves sufficient hepatic parenchyma; resection of segment VII would preserve at least two contiguous segments (I‑II‑III‑VI‑VIII) and is expected to maintain a future liver remnant >30 % of total liver volume. • Technical criteria (negative margins, adequate inflow/outflow, biliary drainage) can be met with a segmentectomy or non‑anatomical wedge resection. • KRAS mutation is a negative prognostic factor but does not preclude curative surgery. Therefore the lesion is technically and oncologically resectable without prerequisite therapy.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Proceed to curative‑intent hepatic resection (segment VII resection or non‑anatomical wedge with ≥1 cm margin) using intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries and exclude occult disease.

Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with four bilobar liver metastases. CEA 900 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion invading the IVC over 1 cm.
MDT Discussion: Caval invasion requiring multidisciplinary surgical evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
- The segment VII metastasis invades the inferior vena cava (IVC) over a length of >1 cm, a situation that generally requires complex vascular reconstruction and careful assessment of oncologic benefit.  
- No information is provided on the future liver remnant (FLR) volume or on the patient’s hepatic functional reserve, which are decisive for any major hepatectomy.  
- Because the FLR assessment is missing and because down‑staging systemic therapy may be needed to reduce tumor burden and improve the chance of an R0 resection with safe margins, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” The prerequisite of a quantified FLR (≥30 % of total liver volume or ≥0.5 % body‑weight) must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be made.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive neoadjuvant systemic therapy: FOLFOXIRI (5‑FU, oxaliplatin, irinotecan) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given the RAS‑wild‑type status, aiming for maximal tumor shrinkage and biologic response assessment.  
- Re‑image the liver (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) after 2–3 cycles (≈6 weeks) to evaluate:  
   • Change in size/number of all metastases, especially the IVC‑invading lesion.  
   • Residual IVC involvement (partial vs. circumferential).  
   • Calculate FLR volume using volumetric software.  
- If FLR is <30 % after anticipated resection, consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy of the future remnant.  
- Should the IVC involvement persist but be limited to a segmental wall, plan for en‑bloc liver resection with segment VII and IVC segment resection followed by prosthetic or autologous graft reconstruction, performed in collaboration with a vascular surgeon.  
- After confirming resectability (R0 achievable, adequate FLR, acceptable vascular reconstruction), adopt a “liver‑first” approach: perform the hepatic resection first while the primary left‑colon tumor is still in situ, provided the patient’s performance status allows.  
- Once the patient recovers from hepatic surgery (≈4–6 weeks), proceed to definitive resection of the primary colon cancer (laparoscopic or open left‑sided colectomy) with appropriate lymphadenectomy.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or continuation of the effective pre‑operative regimen) for a total of 6 months of systemic therapy, adjusted to response and tolerability.  
- Throughout, maintain close MDT surveillance (radiology, oncology, hepatobiliary surgery, vascular surgery, anesthesiology) and consider intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult lesions.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantified future liver remnant (FLR) volume and liver function tests (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, coagulation profile).  
- Detailed extent of IVC invasion (partial wall vs. circumferential, involvement of hepatic veins).  
- Cardiopulmonary reserve and performance status (ECOG/ASA).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants, lymph nodes).  
- Staging details of the primary colon tumor (T stage, nodal status, distance from mesorectal fascia).  
- Baseline comorbidities (cardiac, pulmonary, renal) that could affect major vascular reconstruction.  
- Patient’s preference regarding staged versus simultaneous surgery.

• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (2-4 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 320 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. Positive circulating tumor cells detected.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Six liver metastases (2‑4 cm) are not an absolute contraindication, but the current imaging does not provide:  
  • precise segmental distribution (unilateral vs bilateral)  
  • relationship to major vascular/biliary structures  
  • calculated future liver remnant (FLR) volume  
- The disease is synchronous, CEA is markedly elevated (320 ng/mL) and circulating tumor cells are positive, indicating aggressive biology; guidelines recommend “proof of time” with systemic therapy before committing to surgery.  
- Therefore a prerequisite systemic (neoadjuvant) treatment phase and additional volumetric imaging are required before a definitive surgical plan can be made.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Start 6 cycles of a doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) because the tumour is RAS‑wild‑type and MSS.  
   - Aim for maximal tumour shrinkage and to assess disease biology (response, CTC clearance).  

2. Restaging after induction  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast plus CT of chest/abdomen to:  
     • Re‑evaluate number, size and location of liver lesions  
     • Calculate FLR (target ≥30 % of total liver volume or >0.5 % / kg body weight)  
   - Repeat CEA and circulating tumor cell assay; a decline supports favorable biology.  

3. Decision point  
   - If imaging shows adequate FLR and all lesions are resectable with negative margins → proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery.  
   - If FLR is insufficient → consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy, followed by re‑assessment.  
   - If disease remains extensive or progresses → continue systemic therapy, possibly switch to second‑line regimen, and reassess for conversion or enrolment in a clinical trial.  

4. Surgical sequencing  
   - Because the primary tumour is T4N2, schedule a curative resection of the colon primary (segmental left colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy) either before or concurrently with liver surgery, depending on intra‑operative assessment and patient fitness.  
   - Aim for R0 resection of all hepatic lesions; use intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult disease.  
   - If a single‑stage hepatectomy would leave inadequate FLR, adopt a two‑stage approach:  
     a. First stage – resect lesions in the future liver remnant (e.g., left lateral section) and perform PVE of the right portal branch.  
     b. After 4–6 weeks of hypertrophy, complete right‑hemi hepatectomy (or extended resection) to clear remaining disease.  

5. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   - After surgery, administer adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 3–6 months of the same regimen) unless postoperative pathology shows complete response and patient recovers well, in which case a shorter course may be considered.  

6. Follow‑up  
   - Serial CEA, imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months, and periodic CTC monitoring as a research/prognostic tool.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Detailed liver volumetry (FLR calculation) and segmental location of each metastasis.  
- Vascular/biliary involvement of the lesions (proximity to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, bile ducts).  
- Performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets).  
- Full staging of extra‑hepatic sites (chest CT, PET‑CT) to exclude occult lung or peritoneal disease.  
- Quantitative circulating tumor cell count and trend after systemic therapy.  
- Patient’s preferences regarding the intensity of treatment and willingness for staged hepatic surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six liver metastases (2–4 cm) without reported extrahepatic disease. Despite the bilobar distribution, the number and size of lesions suggest that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. The detection of circulating tumor cells reflects increased systemic risk but does not alter technical resectability. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Mandatory peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the presence of circulating tumor cells indicating systemic dissemination risk, administer 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections of all six lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

E. Management of primary tumor
• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three liver lesions on MRI.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy and long-course pelvic radiotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
E. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
F. Trend and quantification of circulating tumor cells over time.
